answers.answer: Boards sold as termite proof fail, and factory surface treatment weakens at cuts and drill holes; buyers cannot see whether edges were protected.
Homeowners commissioning carpenter-built interiors; local carpenters make most furniture by volume. Which homeowners care enough to pay is not shown.
Once per renovation; failures can appear within two years and damage furniture. How often this happens is not measured.
Branded termite-treated boards, maker advice to treat edges with borate, guarantees from board brands. No verifiable edge-coverage product found.
Unknown. No data on what homeowners or carpenters spend on edge treatment.
Visible proof of edge coverage with a UV torch. Whether buyers value proof enough to pay ₹1,499 is untested.
A past termite failure or a designer who insists on it. Assumption.
Interior designers and contractors; carpenters must agree to apply it. No channel tested.
Modelled at ₹600 per customer; no evidence.
Kit materials about ₹495 plus packing and courier, all assumptions; registration and testing add about ₹4.8 lakh setup.
A 300-kit first batch and 60 inventory days; peak cash need is far above the ₹3 lakh budget in the model.
Pesticide registration time and cost, carpenters skipping it, leaching in wet kitchens, tracer showing through finish, and a negative unit margin once founder time is paid.
Termite infestation complaints on wooden furniture and boards that fail as termite proof suggest board chemistry alone does not protect buyers.
Carpenters and contractors fitting built-ins, and homeowners on termite-prone ground floors. Not validated.
Unknown frequency of termite entry through walls behind built-ins; no data.
Anti-termite soil treatment by pest controllers, termite-treated boards, building-level ant caps (not found for furniture).
Unknown.
Works with any board and makes termite tubes visible early. Research shows shields aid detection more than prevention, which weakens the pitch.
A carpenter who has had termite callbacks. Assumption.
Hardware dealers and carpenter networks; dealer margin is assumed at 25%.
Modelled at ₹800 per carpenter with 3 sets per carpenter; no evidence.
Parts about ₹980 per set plus courier ₹150, assumptions; shipping metal parts is heavy.
200-set batch plus 30-day dealer credit; peak need above budget in the model.
Load and tipping safety, carpenters bridging the gap with trims, low perceived value, and a negative unit margin after dealer cut and acquisition.
Counterfeit plywood and false termite-proof claims mean the board delivered may not be the board promised, and homeowners are rarely on site.
Homeowners with larger renovations who are not on site; size of this group unknown.
Once per renovation; intensity unknown.
Free BIS Care licence check, brand checklists, general home inspection agencies that charge by area.
Unknown. Inspection agencies exist, but no INR prices were found.
An independent check at the moment of delivery, before cutting. Untested.
A bad past experience, or living away from the site. Assumption.
Interior designers and housing societies; designer referral fee assumed at 20%.
Modelled at ₹400 per customer; no evidence.
About 3.3 founder hours per completed visit including travel and wasted trips; travel ₹300 assumed.
Low: about ₹39,000 peak in the model. The constraint is founder time, not cash.
Founder earns about ₹168/hour, below the ₹600/hour opportunity cost; capacity caps at about 30 visits a month; boards can be swapped after inspection; carpenters may resist.
